notes: Phoenix-trading Insolvency Rules 4.230 appeal; Arden LJ's statutory construction and factual findings are detailed and clear.

enrichment.short_title: ESS Production v Sully: rule 4.230 and phoenix company names
key_facts: ESS Fabricating Ltd went into insolvent liquidation in May 1999 while Mr Sully was a director of associated company Electronic Sales Services Ltd.
That company later changed its registered name to ESS Solutions Ltd, a prohibited name, and incurred debts including £21,450.65 to ESS Production Ltd in administration.
The group informally used the acronym ESS on products and correspondence but formal business was conducted in registered company names.
The judge held rule 4.230 did not apply because ESS was not a name under which the company carried on the whole of its business.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from Winchester County Court judgment under section 217 of the Insolvency Act 1986.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and cross-appeal dismissed; the third excepted case in rule 4.230 applied and Mr Sully was not personally liable under section 217.
enrichment.ratio: Rule 4.230 may apply where a company was known by a prohibited name for the whole qualifying period even if that name was an informal trading style or acronym; carrying on business under a name does not require all trading functions to use that name alone, and section 217 liability is limited to relevant debts incurred while the company was known by a prohibited name.
legal_issues: Whether rule 4.230 required the same prohibited registered name throughout the twelve-month qualifying period
Whether a company could carry on business under more than one name for section 216(6) purposes
Whether informal use of the acronym ESS amounted to carrying on business under a prohibited name
The measure of personal liability under section 217(3) for debts incurred under a prohibited name
linked_authorities: Ricketts v Ad Valorem Factors Ltd [2004] 1 BCLC 1
Penrose v Secretary of State for Trade and Industry [1996] 1 WLR 482
Thorne v Silverleaf [1994] 1 BCLC 637

notes: Section 83 certificate of inadequacy application; confiscation realisable property analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: P v HMRC: certificate of inadequacy after cigarette smuggling confiscation
key_facts: The applicant was convicted of smuggling 1.25 million cigarettes and received a confiscation order based on benefit of £187,343.
Equity in a house at 60 Queens Road Hinckley owned by his former partner was treated as realisable property after Mitchell J held £18,933.50 was a caught gift.
The order was reduced to £26,964.83; the applicant paid £20,508.06 but sought a certificate of inadequacy citing a shortfall in an Abbey Life policy surrender value.
The Queens Road property remained outside his control though deemed part of his realisable property.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under section 83(1) of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 for a certificate of inadequacy.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; realisable property was not inadequate because the deemed gift equity exceeded the outstanding balance.
enrichment.ratio: Section 83(2)(b) discretion arises only after the applicant establishes inadequacy of realisable property at the time of the application; gifts treated as realisable property remain relevant even if practically irrecoverable, and the section 83 procedure cannot be used to appeal original gift findings.
legal_issues: Whether realisable property was inadequate after surrender of the Abbey Life policy
Whether equity in Queens Road held to be a caught gift could be disregarded under section 83(2)(b)
Whether the application was an impermissible challenge to earlier confiscation findings
Application of Re May Yoong Forwell to section 83(2)(b)

Gokal v Serious Fraud Office [2001] EWCA Civ 368
Re May Yoong Forwell [2003] EWCA Civ 1608

enrichment.short_title: Ashborder v Green Gas Power: costs after unauthorised permission appeal
key_facts: Claimants sued Green Gas Power, E&P Production and Cabot Energy, companies in provisional or compulsory liquidation.
Mr Garratt maintained an application for permission to appeal Etherton J's decision without authority from the provisional liquidators.
He sought to withdraw the application after learning any appeal had been compromised.
Claimants and provisional liquidators sought costs of £16,775 and £8,886.94 respectively.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal hearing on whether to dismiss or permit withdrawal of an application for permission to appeal and on third-party costs orders.
enrichment.outcome: Application for permission to appeal dismissed; Mr Garratt ordered to pay claimants £9,947 and provisional liquidators £8,086 in costs from 28 January 2005.
enrichment.ratio: A person who purports to act for a company in provisional liquidation without liquidator authority may routinely be ordered to pay other parties' costs on an indemnity basis; a lay litigant who continued after clear warnings and knew the appeal was settled remains liable for substantial costs.
legal_issues: Whether to dismiss or permit withdrawal of the permission application
Whether Mr Garratt had authority to pursue the application after provisional liquidators were appointed
The appropriate costs order and period from which costs should run
Application of Pacific & General Insurance v Hazell to unauthorised solicitors

notes: Extradition Act 2003 MDMA criminality ground; Sedley LJ's foreign-law analysis is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Bentley v United States: extradition failed on MDMA proscription proof
key_facts: Richard Bentley was accused of conspiring from the UK to import MDMA ecstasy tablets to Florida for Keith Reilly.
The US request relied on expert evidence that MDMA was a Schedule I controlled substance but exhibited statutes not listing the chemical at the material time.
A temporary 1985 CFR scheduling measure had expired by 1987 and no permanent proscription was proved to the criminal standard.
The district judge had assumed MDMA remained banned; the Home Secretary ordered extradition.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 103 of the Extradition Act 2003 against a district judge's decision to send the case to the Home Secretary.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on the criminality ground; Mr Bentley discharged and the extradition order quashed.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 137(2)(c) the requesting state must prove to the criminal standard that the conduct was punishable under its law at the material time; where volunteered documents undermine the expert assertion that MDMA was proscribed, the court cannot presume criminalisation, even for category 2 territories benefiting from a prima facie case waiver.
legal_issues: Whether MDMA was a controlled substance in US federal law in 2003-2004
Whether UK conduct amounted to an extradition offence under section 137
Whether extraterritorial conspiracy liability satisfied section 137(2)(a)
Whether extradition was compatible with Article 8 ECHR

Somchai Liangsiriprasert v Government of the United States [1991] 1 AC 225

notes: Landfill PPC permit JR; Sullivan J's EU directive interpretation on hydraulic containment is comprehensive.

enrichment.short_title: Lewis v Environment Agency: New Albion landfill PPC permit upheld

statutes_considered.title: Pollution Prevention and Control (England and Wales) Regulations 2000

key_facts: The Environment Agency granted Onyx a PPC permit for the New Albion sub-water table landfill site near Ashby de la Zouch.
The site would accept up to 600,000 tonnes of waste per year using hydraulic containment with a clay liner and leachate pumping.
The claimant challenged groundwater ingress, fit-and-proper-person financial provision, reliance on pumping as a technical precaution, and leachate treatment conditions.
Sub-water table landfills with inward hydraulic gradients are common in the Midlands and elsewhere in the EU.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a PPC permit granted under Regulation 10 of the PPC Regulations 2000.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed on all four grounds; permission granted on grounds (2) and (4) but substantive challenge failed.
enrichment.ratio: Annex I of the Landfill Directive requires groundwater to be prevented from entering landfilled waste in an engineering sense, not absolutely; a designed clay liner maintaining an inward hydraulic gradient prevents prohibited direct discharge of list I substances under the Groundwater Directive, and deferred leachate treatment specification may be lawful if the Agency is satisfied appropriate measures will be taken.
legal_issues: Whether hydraulic containment breached Annex I paragraph 2 of the Landfill Directive
Whether inward groundwater flow constituted direct discharge of list I substances
Whether reliance on leachate pumping was an impermissible technical precaution
Whether financial provision for aftercare beyond 60 years was adequate under Article 8(a)(iv)
linked_authorities: R v Vale of Glamorgan BC ex p James [1996] Env LR 102
Commission v Germany [1991] ECR I-00825

notes: Christie's Houghton vases appeal; May LJ reconciled inconsistent breach-of-duty finding with non-negligent cataloguing.

enrichment.short_title: Thomson v Christie's: Louis XV vases catalogue negligence appeal
key_facts: Ms Thomson bought a pair of porphyry and gilt-bronze vases catalogued as Louis XV at Christie's 1994 Houghton sale for nearly £2 million.
Jack J found the vases were probably 18th century but held Christie's breached a special duty to Ms Thomson despite finding cataloguing not negligent.
Metallurgical evidence later cast doubt on dating; electrolytic gilding of liners raised a possible 19th-century query.
Christie's appealed the breach finding and damages measure; Ms Thomson cross-appealed on dating and catalogue qualification.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from Jack J's judgment on negligence and misrepresentation claims against Christie's.
enrichment.outcome: Christie's appeal allowed and Ms Thomson's cross-appeal dismissed; no breach of duty and the misrepresentation claim failed.
enrichment.ratio: Where an auctioneer is not negligent in a confident catalogue description, it is inconsistent to find breach of a special client duty absent a real doubt requiring qualification; later gilding of liners did not raise more than a fanciful doubt about 18th-century dating on the judge's findings.
legal_issues: Whether Christie's were in breach of a special duty despite non-negligent cataloguing
The correct measure of damages if breach were established
Whether the vases should have been described as probably Louis XV
Whether electrolytic liner gilding required catalogue qualification
linked_authorities: Thomson v Christie Manson & Woods Ltd [2004] EWHC 1101 (QB)

notes: Harry Stanley inquest JR; Collins J quashed unlawful killing verdict for insufficient evidence on self-defence belief.

enrichment.short_title: Sharman v Inner North London Coroner: Harry Stanley unlawful killing quashed
key_facts: Henry Stanley was shot dead by armed police in Hackney in September 1999 after a 999 call reported a man with a sawn-off shotgun in a blue bag.
The object was a table leg; Chief Inspector Sharman fired the fatal shot and Constable Fagan wounded Mr Stanley's hand.
A second inquest returned unlawful killing; forensic evidence cast doubt on the officers' detailed account of Mr Stanley's movements.
Chief Inspector Sharman sought judicial review of the verdict on Galbraith insufficiency grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a coroner's jury verdict of unlawful killing after a mandatory inquest under section 8 of the Coroners' Act 1988.
enrichment.outcome: Verdict of unlawful killing quashed; narrative findings on time, place and circumstances preserved; no further inquest ordered.
enrichment.ratio: A verdict of unlawful killing at an inquest requires evidence on which a jury could safely conclude beyond reasonable doubt that the officer did not honestly believe he or another officer faced imminent threat of being shot; rejection of the officers' account of movements does not automatically rebut subjective self-defence without more.
legal_issues: Whether there was sufficient evidence to leave unlawful killing to the jury
Whether rejection of the officers' account necessarily implied lack of honest belief in imminent threat
Whether the summing up adequately directed the jury on ingredients of unlawful killing
Article 2 requirements for inquests into deaths caused by police use of force
linked_authorities: R v HM Coroner for Exeter ex parte Palmer (1997)
R v Inner South London Coroner ex parte Douglas-Williams [1999] 1 All ER 344
Jordan v United Kingdom (2003) 37 EHRR 2

notes: ASBO and burglary sentence appeal; David Clarke J applied Shane Tony P principles clearly.

enrichment.short_title: R v Rush: reduced sentence and five-year ASBO for parental burglary
key_facts: The appellant pushed past his father into his parents' home and stole a packet of cigarettes after being ejected from the family home.
He had a long history of offences against his parents including harassment and a recent community punishment for a similar burglary.
The judge sentenced him to two-and-a-half years' imprisonment consecutive to five months already served and made a ten-year ASBO.
The ASBO prohibited conduct causing alarm or distress to his parents and any contact with them.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence and criminal Anti-Social Behaviour Order imposed in the Crown Court at Newcastle.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; prison sentence reduced to twelve months and ASBO duration reduced from ten to five years.
enrichment.ratio: Even for persistent harassment of family victims, a low-value burglary sentence may be excessive when coupled with an ASBO; a criminal ASBO requires demonstrable necessity and its duration must be carefully justified, though focused protection of identified victims can be appropriate.
legal_issues: Whether thirty months' imprisonment was manifestly excessive for the burglary
Whether a criminal ASBO was necessary alongside custody
The appropriate duration of an ASBO where the offender will be on licence
Application of R v Shane Tony P to ASBO necessity
linked_authorities: R v Shane Tony P [2004] 2 Cr App R(S) 63

enrichment.short_title: Sinclair v Versailles: fiduciary duty and fraud trust pleading appeal
key_facts: Sinclair invested £2.35 million with TPL under Versailles Group accelerated discount trading agreements requiring unused funds to be held on trust.
It alleged Mr Cushnie personally assured traders their funds were ring-fenced while the group fraudulently inflated turnover to profit from share sales.
Claims included personal fiduciary duties owed by Mr Cushnie and a constructive trust over profits from Marrlist share sales.
VTFL appealed a deputy judge's refusal to strike out amended particulars permitting those claims to proceed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against partial allowance of an appeal from Master Bowman's refusal to strike out claims and grant of permission to amend.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; fiduciary relationship and alternative fraud-based constructive trust claims may proceed to trial.
enrichment.ratio: A director may owe a personal fiduciary duty of loyalty to an investor where pleaded assurances show he undertook to monitor and protect that investor's funds separately from the company; an arguable claim may also lie that a stranger who profited from fraudulent misuse of trust monies holds profits on constructive trust even where conventional tracing is unavailable.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Cushnie owed parallel fiduciary duties to Sinclair beyond TPL's obligations
Whether amended pleadings sufficiently alleged assumption of a duty of loyalty
Whether a constructive trust arises over profits from fraudulent share dealings without tracing
The correct approach to strike-out in developing areas of equity

notes: Ivory Coast asylum appeal; Scott Baker LJ held credibility error material where medical reports not considered in the round.

enrichment.short_title: Diaby v SSHD: remittal after material credibility and medical evidence error
key_facts: Mr Diaby, an Ivorian Malinki and alleged RDR member, claimed detention and torture by military and rebels before fleeing via Ghana to the UK.
The adjudicator found him not credible before considering GP and psychiatric reports submitted after the hearing.
Reports recorded burn scars and eye injury consistent with his account and post-traumatic stress symptoms.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal dismissed his appeal without examining the medical evidence on the file.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Immigration Appeal Tribunal dismissal of an asylum and human rights appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted to a fresh tribunal for reconsideration.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator errs in law by forming an adverse credibility finding before considering all evidence including late medical reports; where those reports bear on scarring, eye injury and demeanour, the error may be material even if other credibility concerns remain.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator's approach to late medical evidence was an error of law
Whether the IAT erred in assessing materiality without reviewing the medical reports
Whether burn scars and eye injury evidence could affect credibility findings
Proper procedure when representatives fail to adduce evidence before the IAT
